observations:
Torah #183 is a very short teaching (6 sentences) yielding only 3 bechina edges across 6 nodes. After the principled merge of the two love-vision components, the teaching reduces to exactly 2 packages, which fully account for the Torah's entire conceptual content.

Candidate clusters examined and rejected:

1. SUSTENANCE/JUDGMENT (פרנסה, מזונות, משפטים): These concepts appear prominently in the text — the tzaddikim distribute sustenance and issue judgments to every person. However, their relationship to the tzaddikim-court is eitza (causal flow), not bechina. The text says 'from them go out all judgments and all sustenance' — this is a directional production, not a shared essential nature. Parnasa and mishpat are outputs of the court, not faces of the same thing as the court. They cannot form a bechina-based package.

2. SANHEDRIN / GOREN / CIRCLE (סנהדרין, גורן עגולה, ישיבה בעיגול): These three concepts appear together in the closing verse-interpretation (line 6) and all relate to the structural/institutional expression of the tzaddikim. However, upon examination: סנהדרין is a bechina of the tzaddikim-court (Package 1), גורן עגולה is a bechina of the tzaddikim-circle as source of sustenance (Package 1), and ישיבה בעיגול is a bechina of seeing one another (Package 2). They distribute naturally into the two existing packages by shared essential nature and do not form a third independent domain. Three nodes that each connect to different existing packages do not constitute a new package.

3. EVIL MIRROR (שנאה, 'cannot look at'): The text mentions the negative pole — hatred is defined as 'not being able to look at something' — as a contrast to establish the love-seeing identity. However, שנאה receives only passing implicit mention as the negation of love, not as a fully developed bechina concept with its own cluster. There is no evil mirror package in this Torah — the teaching is a compact positive statement about the tzaddikim's love, not a dual-polarity argument.

Conclusion: Torah #183 is a tight, focused teaching with exactly two conceptual domains — (1) the tzaddikim-as-court structure, and (2) the identity of love and vision. All bechina-language in the text is accountable within these two packages. The teaching's architecture is: the tzaddikim sit in a circle [Package 1 structure] so that they see one another [Package 2 principle], which constitutes love [Package 2]. The circle = the court [Package 1], which is sanctioned by the Sanhedrin precedent [addition to Package 1]. No new independent domain of 3+ bechina-connected concepts exists outside these two packages.
